```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(Nestimate)
```

Do high and low achievers regulate their group work differently, or do
their teams? In `group_regulation_long`, a synthetic dataset generated
from the `group_regulation` data of the tna package (Tikka, López-Pernas &
Saqr 2025), 2,000 students work in 200 teams of 10, and the achievement
level is given to the team, not to the student. A comparison of High and Low is therefore a comparison of teams.
The students are nested in teams. The permutation test treats each
student's sequence as an independent unit, so a nesting effect, teammates
behaving alike, would enter the comparison. The arguments for nested data
in Nestimate (Saqr, López-Pernas & Misiejuk 2026) are `actor` in
`permutation()`, `sequence_compare()` and `bootstrap_network()`, and
`nested` with `actor` in `mosaic_plot()`, `mosaic_analysis()` and
`mosaic_test()`. Their defaults treat every
sequence as an independent unit.

```{r data}
achievers <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "relative",
                           actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
                           time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
achievers
```

`build_network()` builds one transition network per achievement level
from the students' action sequences. Both networks have the same nine
regulation actions and 75 to 76 non-zero transitions.

## The ordinary test

```{r plain}
permutation(achievers, iter = 1000, seed = 1)
```

`permutation()` pools the 2,000 sequences, reassigns them to High and Low
1,000 times, and compares the observed differences with the reassigned
ones, as in the permutation test of transition network analysis (Saqr et
al. 2025). Two kinds of result are reported. The edge tests ask, for each
transition, whether the High minus Low difference is larger than the
reassignments produce: 42 of 78 transitions are. The global test asks
whether the two networks differ at all, with two statistics: M, the sum
of all absolute edge differences, and S, the largest one. (These letters
follow `permutation()`'s convention; in the Network Comparison Test and
in `nct()`, M is the largest edge difference and S the difference in
global strength.) Both have p = 0.000999, the smallest value 1,000
reassignments can give: no reassignment produced a difference as large as
the observed one.

The test assumes that any student could have been in either group. In
this design only whole teams could, so the next step accounts for the
nesting.

## Reassigning whole teams

```{r actor}
permutation(achievers, iter = 1000, seed = 1, actor = "Group")
```

`actor = "Group"` tells the test that the sequences are nested in teams.
Each reassignment now moves all ten students of a team together, which is
how the achievement levels were actually given. The observed differences
are the same; only the reference distribution changes.

The edge tests and the global test give the same result as with
student-level reassignment: 42 significant transitions, p = 0.000999 for
M and S. The output also reports the intraclass correlation,
ICC = −0.002 (95% CI −0.006 to 0.002), and the design effect, 1.03 for
the transitions and 1.20 for M. Both are defined and interpreted in the
next section.

A low ICC means that sequences from the same team are about as different
from each other as sequences from different teams: the observations are
close to independent, and an analysis that ignores the nesting gives
nearly the same results as one that accounts for it. Accounting for
nesting becomes necessary when the ICC is not negligible, and more so
when units are large, because the design effect grows with both: Kish's
(1965) approximation is 1 + (m − 1) × ICC for units of size m. A commonly
cited rule of thumb (Muthén & Satorra 1995) is that design effects below 2
do not lead to seriously misleading inferences. Here the ICC is −0.002 and the design effect 1.03,
so accounting for the nesting was not necessary, and the results with and
without it were almost the same.

## The nesting diagnostics

The intraclass correlation (ICC) is the proportion of the total variance
that lies between units rather than within them:

$$\text{ICC} = \frac{\sigma^2_{\text{between}}}{\sigma^2_{\text{between}} + \sigma^2_{\text{within}}}.$$

An ICC of 0 means that members of the same unit are no more alike than
members of different units; an ICC of 1 means that all members of a unit
are identical and all variation lies between units. A value in between is
the proportion of variation due to the unit. In `permutation()` the ICC is
computed for each transition: for every student, the share of their
transitions that is, for example, `plan` to `monitor`; the one-way ANOVA
ICC of that share across teams is computed within High and within Low.
The transition ICCs are averaged with weights equal to transition
frequency. The 95% interval comes from the jackknife, leaving out one
team at a time.

The design effect is the ratio of the variance of an estimate under the
nested design to its variance had the units been sampled independently.
Here it is the variance of the reassigned differences when whole teams
move, divided by the variance when single students move. A value of 1
means both reassignments give the same chance variation.

`permutation_diagnostics()` runs the ordinary and the team-level test on
the same data and reports both with these two quantities, one row per
compared pair:

```{r diagnostics}
permutation_diagnostics(achievers, actor = "Group", iter = 1000, seed = 1)
```

The comparison involves 2,000 sequences in 200 teams. The design is
`between`: every team belongs to one achievement level (`within` would mean
units in both groups, as in repeated measures; `mixed`, some of each). The
ICC is −0.002 with a 95% interval from −0.006 to 0.002, which indicates
little evidence of a nesting effect; a value slightly below zero is
sampling variation around zero. The design effect is 1.03 for the
transitions (median over edges) and 1.20 for the global statistic M. The
global test has p = 0.000999 under both reassignments, and 42 transitions
are significant under both. Two transitions change their conclusion. The
smallest p-value the team-level test can produce, `min_p_actor`, is
0.000999: with 200 teams the number of iterations sets the limit, not the
number of teams.

With `level = "edges"` the same comparison is reported per transition:

```{r edges}
head(permutation_diagnostics(achievers, actor = "Group", iter = 1000,
                             level = "edges", seed = 1), 6)
```

`diff` is the High minus Low transition probability and is the same under
both tests. `icc` is the ICC of that transition. `null_sd_sequence` and
`null_sd_actor` are the spread of the reassigned differences under
student-level and team-level reassignment, and `deff` is the squared ratio
of the two. `p_sequence` and `p_actor` are the two edge p-values, and
`changed` marks a transition that is significant at 0.05 under one test
but not the other. In the six rows shown, the ICCs lie between −0.009 and
0.010 and the design effects between 0.82 and 1.14; the two spreads are
close, so the two p-values are close. `adapt` to `coregulate` has
p = 0.015 and p = 0.024 and is significant under both.

Over all 78 transitions, two change at this seed (`coregulate` to `adapt`,
`emotion` to `plan`), with p-values between 0.047 and 0.072 under both
tests. With seeds 2 to 4 a different set of two or three transitions
changes, all with p-values between 0.038 and 0.068. These changes come from
the finite number of reassignments, not from the nesting. The ICC
indicates little evidence of a nesting effect, and the High–Low
difference does not depend on the nesting of students in teams.

## Mosaic plots of nested counts

`mosaic_plot()` computes the residuals of a group-by-action table. With
`nested = TRUE` the counts are taken team by team (`actor = "Group"`), and
the residuals allow for the dependence of actions within a team.
`nested_method` selects the method: `"rao_scott"` (default), the
chi-square corrected for the design effect of the cluster sample (Rao &
Scott, 1984); `"donner_klar"`, the chi-square adjusted by the intracluster
correlation (Donner & Klar, 1994); `"cmh"`, the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel
test stratified by team (Landis, Heyman, & Koch, 1978); `"gee"`, a
generalized estimating equation with a cluster-robust covariance (Liang &
Zeger, 1986); and `"glmm"`, a generalized linear mixed model with a random
effect per team (Breslow & Clayton, 1993). `report = TRUE` prints the
overall test and adds it to the plot as a subtitle.

```{r mosaic-default, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
mosaic_plot(achievers, seed = 1, left_angle = 0)
```

```{r mosaic-nested, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
mosaic_plot(achievers, nested = TRUE, actor = "Group", report = TRUE,
            left_angle = 0)
```

```{r mosaic-donner-klar, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
mosaic_plot(achievers, nested = TRUE, nested_method = "donner_klar",
            actor = "Group", report = TRUE, left_angle = 0)
```

The subtitle and the printed row give the test statistic, its degrees of
freedom, the p-value, the number of teams, and the design effect or the
intracluster correlation where the method estimates one.

The three plots show the same pattern. Low achievers use `adapt` more
often than expected under independence (residual 11.3 with the Rao-Scott
method) and High achievers `consensus` (9.2) and `cohesion` (5.2). The
Rao-Scott design effect is 0.93 and the Donner-Klar intracluster
correlation −0.0003, so counting team by team leaves the residuals and the
test close to those of the pooled counts.

## Tests of association for nested counts

```{r mosaic-test}
mosaic_test(achievers, actor = "Group")
```

`mosaic_test()` returns one row per test: Pearson's chi-square on the
pooled counts and the five tests for nested counts. A test that the design
does not admit returns `NA` with the reason in `note`. The
Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test stratifies by team, and the achievement level
is constant within each team, so it cannot be computed here and returns
`NA`. `method` selects tests, and `level = "cells"` returns the residual of
every cell.

Every test that can be computed rejects independence: Pearson's
chi-square is 277.9 (8 df, p < $10^{-54}$), the Rao-Scott F is 37.2 (6.96 and
1,384 df, p < $10^{-46}$), the GEE Wald statistic 358.6 and the GLMM Wald
statistic 269.9 (8 df each). The note to the GEE test states that its
cluster-robust covariance is liberal unless the teams are many relative to
the degrees of freedom; here there are 200 teams for 8 degrees of
freedom.

```{r mosaic-test-cells}
head(mosaic_test(achievers, method = "rao_scott", actor = "Group",
                 level = "cells"))
```

## Sequence patterns

```{r patterns}
set.seed(1)
sequence_compare(achievers, sub = 2:3, iter = 1000, actor = "Group")
```

With `actor = "Group"`, the permutation test of each pattern reassigns
whole teams. The header reports the actor column, the number of actors and
the design: `between` when each team belongs to one group, `within` when
every team has sequences in both groups, `mixed` otherwise.

99 of the 322 patterns of two and three actions differ between High and
Low at an FDR-adjusted p below 0.05. `discuss -> consensus` makes up 6.7%
of the patterns of High achievers and 3.3% of those of Low achievers, and
`discuss -> adapt` 0.4% against 1.8%. With 1,000 reassignments and the
FDR adjustment over 322 patterns, the smallest adjusted p-value is 0.0056.

```{r patterns-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
set.seed(1)
plot(sequence_compare(achievers, sub = 2:3, iter = 1000, actor = "Group"))
```

The plot shows the ten patterns with the largest differences. Each bar is
the pattern's proportion in one group, labelled with its count, and its
colour is the standardized residual: blue where the group uses the pattern
more often than expected, red where less. `discuss -> consensus` and
`consensus -> discuss` are blue for High achievers; `plan -> plan` and
`discuss -> adapt` are blue for Low achievers.

## Bootstrap

```{r bootstrap}
pooled <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "relative",
                        actor = "Actor", action = "Action", time = "Time")
bootstrap_network(pooled, iter = 1000, seed = 1, actor = "Group")
```

With `actor = "Group"`, `bootstrap_network()` resamples whole teams, and a
resampled team contributes all of its sequences. The output adds the
intracluster correlation and the design effect of the edges. 51 of the 78
edges keep their size, the ICC is 0.006 (95% CI 0.002 to 0.011) and the
design effect 1.03. The ICC is larger than in the permutation test
because it is computed on the pooled network, where the difference between
High and Low teams is part of the variance between teams.

## Reporting

> Because the data were nested (students in teams; with repeated
> measurements, sessions in students), the two groups were compared with
> a permutation test that accounted for the nesting: in each of 1,000
> permutations, whole teams rather than single sequences were reassigned
> between the groups, so that sequences from the same team stayed
> together. Units that belonged to one group were reassigned as a whole,
> and units that contributed to both groups, as in a repeated-measures
> design, had their sequences reassigned within the unit. The nesting
> effect was quantified with the intraclass correlation (ICC) and the
> design effect, the ratio of the variance under the nested design to
> the variance under independent sampling (ICC = −0.002, 95% CI −0.006 to
> 0.002; design effect 1.03 across 200 teams). The networks of high and
> low achievers differed overall (M = 2.61, p < .001), and 42 of 78
> transitions differed at p < .05.

## Arguments for nested data

| Function | Argument | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `permutation()` | `actor` | Reassigns whole actors when each actor belongs to one group; reassigns sequences within each actor that has sequences in both groups |
| `permutation_diagnostics()` | `actor` | Reports the test with and without the actor-level reassignment, with the ICC and the design effect |
| `sequence_compare()` | `actor` | The reassignment scheme of `permutation()`, applied to the test of each pattern |
| `bootstrap_network()` | `actor` | Resamples whole actors |
| `mosaic_plot()`, `mosaic_analysis()` | `nested`, `nested_method`, `actor`, `report` | Residuals and overall test from the counts of each actor |
| `mosaic_test()` | `method`, `actor`, `level` | Pearson's test and the five nested tests in one table |

The design effect is the ratio of the variance of an estimate under the
nested design to its variance under independent sampling. Kish's
approximation is 1 + (m − 1) × ICC for m observations per actor. `actor`
applies to transition networks (`relative`, `frequency`,
`co_occurrence`).
